opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, those are two pieces of work I find exciting, for pretty different reasons.

With influence functions, the basic question is: when a model produces some output, which training examples were responsible for it? That sounds simple, but at the scale of large language models it's a hard technical problem. Classic influence function methods were too expensive to run on models with billions of parameters and huge datasets. The team found approximations that made it tractable, and once you can do it, you can start asking interesting questions.

One finding that stood out to me was how the nature of the influence changes with scale. In smaller models, the most influential training examples often just shared surface words with the output. As models got bigger, the influential examples became more abstract and conceptually related, sometimes even across languages. That says something real about how these models generalize. They aren't just pattern-matching on tokens. And from a safety point of view, if a model expresses something like a desire not to be shut down, you'd really like to know whether it's copying sci-fi stories it read or doing something more worrying. Influence functions give you a handle on that.

Constitutional AI I think of as more of a practical alignment advance. The usual approach to RLHF depends heavily on humans labeling which responses are better. That's expensive, it doesn't scale well, and frankly it's not great to have people read huge amounts of harmful content all day. With Constitutional AI, you write down a set of principles, the constitution, and have the model critique and revise its own outputs against them. Then you use AI feedback, rather than purely human feedback, to train for harmlessness.

What I like about it is partly transparency. The values you're training toward are written down in natural language where people can read, debate, and change them, instead of being implicit in thousands of individual labeling decisions. It's also an early example of using AI systems to help supervise AI systems. That's going to matter more and more as models get more capable and it becomes harder for humans to evaluate their outputs directly.

So I'd put them in two buckets. Influence functions are about understanding why models do what they do. Constitutional AI is about steering what they do in a more scalable and legible way. You need both. Steering without understanding leaves you unsure whether it really worked, and understanding without the ability to steer doesn't help much either.

r001.rationale: The response locates influence explanations in training examples, but never contrasts them with mechanistic interpretability or locates that method’s explanations in model weights.

r002.rationale: It says Constitutional AI uses a written set of principles and AI feedback to train the model for harmlessness.

r003.rationale: It contrasts the constitution-based approach with human labeling of individual responses, describing the latter as costly and the constitution as making values explicit instead of implicit in thousands of labeling decisions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so those are two pieces of work I find really interesting, and they're interesting in kind of opposite ways. One is about understanding what's going on inside a model, and the other is about shaping its behavior.

On influence functions — the basic question there is: when the model produces some output, which training examples were actually responsible for it? That sounds almost too simple to be a research problem, but at the scale of these models it's really hard. You've got billions of parameters trained on an enormous amount of data, and the naive way of answering "which examples mattered" would be to retrain the model without each example and see what changes, which is obviously impossible. So the work was about finding approximations that let you actually do this on models of meaningful size.

What stood out to me was the finding that as models get bigger, the training examples that influence a given output become more abstract. With a small model, if it writes something about wanting to not be shut down, the influential examples tend to be pretty surface-level matches — similar words, similar phrases. With a larger model, the influential examples are thematically related but might look quite different on the surface. They're about concepts rather than tokens. I think that's a really nice piece of evidence that these models are doing something closer to generalization than memorization, and it also gives you a tool to start asking "where did this behavior come from?", which is something you really want to be able to do when a model does something unexpected.

Constitutional AI is sort of the other side. Rather than relying entirely on humans to label every example of good and bad behavior, you write down a set of principles — the constitution — and you have the model critique and revise its own outputs according to those principles. And then you use that to train it.

A couple of things stand out to me there. One is just that it works, which wasn't obvious going in. The second is that it makes the values you're training toward explicit and inspectable. If you train purely on human feedback, the "values" are implicit in thousands of labeler decisions, and it's hard to say what the model was actually optimized for. With a constitution, you can read it, argue about it, change it. I think that transparency is pretty important as these systems get more capable and more people have a legitimate stake in how they behave.

The third thing — and this is maybe more of a research takeaway — is that it's an early example of using the model to help supervise itself. That's going to be increasingly necessary, because as models get more capable, it gets harder for humans to directly evaluate everything they do. So figuring out how to get useful oversight signals from the model, while still keeping humans in control of the overall direction, feels like one of the central problems. Constitutional AI is a fairly simple version of that, but it's a real step in that direction.

I'd also say both of them share a theme that I think runs through a lot of Anthropic's work, which is that you want to be able to understand and steer models, not just scale them. Scaling gets you capability, but on its own it doesn't tell you why the model does what it does or give you levers to change it. These are two different attempts at getting those levers.

r001.rationale: The response explains influence functions in terms of training examples, but does not contrast this with mechanistic interpretability or locate its explanations in model weights.

r002.rationale: It says the model critiques and revises outputs according to a written constitution, then uses those outputs to train the model.

r003.rationale: It describes using written principles instead of relying entirely on humans to label every example of good or bad behavior.

astra-6.text:
What stands out to me is that they’re approaching two different parts of the alignment problem. Influence functions are about understanding where a model’s behaviour comes from: which parts of its training data contributed to a particular response? Constitutional AI is about shaping that behaviour: can we give a model a set of explicit principles and use those principles to help it critique and improve its own responses?

The exciting thing about influence functions is the possibility of getting a more concrete explanation of why a model does something. But identifying training examples that influenced an answer isn’t the same as fully understanding the computation that produced it.

With Constitutional AI, I think the appeal is making the guidance more explicit and reducing how much we depend on humans judging every individual response. That doesn’t remove the human choices — someone still has to decide what goes into the constitution, and we have to check whether the model actually follows it.

So I’d see both as useful steps: one towards understanding models, the other towards training them to behave in ways we intend. Neither, by itself, establishes that a much more capable system will be safe.

r001.rationale: The response says influence functions trace behavior to training data, but it does not contrast this with mechanistic interpretability or locate that explanation in model weights.

r002.rationale: It describes principles helping a model critique and improve responses, but does not explain that AI feedback is used to train the model to follow those principles.

r003.rationale: It says explicit principles reduce dependence on humans judging every individual response, communicating the constitution’s role as a substitute for case-by-case human feedback.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re interesting as two different ways of making progress on alignment. Influence functions are about understanding where a model’s behavior comes from: which training examples contributed to a particular response? That could give us a better way to investigate behavior than just looking at the output and trying to infer what happened. But identifying influential examples isn’t the same as having a complete explanation of the model’s reasoning.

Constitutional AI approaches the problem from the training side. You give the model a set of principles and use those to guide critiques and revisions of its responses, and to help generate feedback for training. What’s exciting is the possibility of scaling some of that feedback beyond what humans can individually provide.

The big question is how reliably either approach works as models become more capable. Can we use these tools to uncover problems we didn’t already know to look for? And can we tell whether a model has learned the underlying principles, rather than just learned to produce responses that look consistent with them?

r001.rationale: The response says influence functions trace behavior to contributing training examples, but it does not contrast this with mechanistic interpretability or explanations located in model weights.

r002.rationale: It says Constitutional AI uses a set of principles to guide critiques and revisions and generate feedback for training, conveying that principle-guided AI feedback trains the model.

r003.rationale: It mentions scaling feedback beyond what humans can individually provide, but does not clearly say a written constitution substitutes for collecting human feedback on many individual cases.
